Palatial

/puh-LAY-shul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Palatial means resembling a palace in grand size and luxury.

The opera house lobby was palatial, all marble columns, gilded balconies, and chandeliers the size of rowboats.

Worked Example

When the twins inherited their great-aunt's country house, they expected a cottage. Instead they found a palatial residence: a ballroom lined with gilded mirrors, a dining hall that seated forty, twin marble staircases, and grounds that took an hour to walk. Visitors kept asking whether royalty had ever lived there, because everything about the place was built on the scale of a palace.

The house's enormous size, grand rooms, and luxurious details make it resemble a palace, which is exactly what palatial means.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

Where it sits · how grand and vast it is — spacious → palatial → monumental

spacious vs. palatial: A spacious room simply offers plenty of space, while a palatial one carries the sweeping grandeur and luxury of a palace.

monumental vs. palatial: A palatial mansion imitates the luxury of a palace, but a monumental structure is built on a scale so colossal that it dwarfs everything around it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — palat

Root — palat: from Latin palatium, palace, named after the Palatine Hill in Rome

Suffix — -ial

Suffix — -ial: characteristic of (a form of the suffix -al)

Put it together

Put it together: Palatial attaches the -ial form of the suffix -al, 'characteristic of,' to Latin palatium, 'palace.' The word palatium itself comes from the Palatine Hill in Rome, where the emperor Augustus built his residence; the hill's name became the word for any grand home, and palatial means characteristic of one.

Use the root in a new word: Palatine

Use the root in a new word: Palatine: Tourists climbing the Palatine Hill in Rome walk the very ground whose name gave English both palace and palatial, because the emperor Augustus built his residence there.

Word Choice

descriptive, journalistic register

Palatial describes physical grandeur only: buildings, rooms, estates, and lobbies that look and feel like palaces. It does not describe a person's wealth or behavior, and it is not a synonym for expensive; a tiny diamond costs a fortune, but nothing about it is palatial.
